Low drought tolerance, languishes in the summer heat.' — and Clemson only advises watering 'on a regular basis' in fall and winter. is_houseplant false: no admissible source states Antirrhinum majus is grown or marketed as a houseplant. RHS's own Hardiness Ratings legend defines H2 as 'tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5)', a frost-sensitivity band; the greenhouse/under-glass wording the original entry attached to H2 belongs to a different band on that legend (H1A), not to this one, and is not indoor houseplant culture.

It is now cited here for common_name, name_note, outdoor_sun_exposure and is_houseplant. Nothing on it contradicts a landed value: its 'Soil tolerances: acidic; slightly alkaline; clay; sand; loam' is a qualitative list with no numeric bounds, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max stay null. records.name_note: Sources converge on Silver Ragwort at the page-lead level, with dusty miller as the common alternative. NC State's Common Name(s) list is a stacked pair, 'Dusty Miller' then 'Silver Ragwort', matching its page-title parenthetical order. Missouri Botanical Garden renders a single Common Name field whose value is 'silver ragwort'. RHS's dedicated Plant Profile renders the heading 'Jacobaea maritima' with 'silver ragwort' as the rendered subtitle immediately beneath it, and places dusty miller only in its secondary Other common names field ('dusty miller, sea ragwort'). Two of the three dedicated pages lead with silver ragwort, so that is the landed name. On the accepted name: RHS marks Jacobaea maritima's Name Status Correct and Senecio cineraria's Synonym, and NC State's Previously known as list carries Senecio cineraria, so the Senecio name is followed through to Jacobaea maritima.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Jacobaea maritima page flags the record at the top with 'This plant has high severity poison characteristics.' and carries a human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block: Poison Severity 'High'; Poison Symptoms 'All parts of this plant are toxic if ingested. It can cause serious liver damage. Minor skin irritation can occur following contact, but lasts for only a few minutes.'; Poison Toxic Principle 'Pyrrolizidine alkaloids.'; Causes Contact Dermatitis 'Yes'; and a Poison Part list of six stacked values — Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice — which is the complete list. Its description adds an explicit handling warning: 'If ingested, dusty miller is toxic to pets and humans. Skin irritation may occur when handling this plant. Protective clothing and gloves are recommended.' The Problems field co-lists five tags — Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses — and it is the separate Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags, not the human-scoped severity rating, that set toxic_to_pets true. NC State also carries 'Poisonous' as one of the two Whole Plant Traits Plant Type values alongside 'Herbaceous Perennial', and its Edibility field reads 'Toxic if ingested.' RHS's page adds only a genus-level description of Jacobaea noting the genus is 'primarily known as being toxic to horses and cattle'; that is boilerplate about roughly 35 species, not species-specific evidence, and it does not bear on cats or dogs.
unknowns: is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames Jacobaea maritima as an indoor houseplant in its own right. NC State mentions groundcover use 'in interiorscapes' inside one mixed list — 'interiorscapes, forests or natural areas, patios, or in garden beds and borders' — and tags the page #interiorscape, which is disclosed here as the one contrary mention; against it, NC State's Plant Type values are Herbaceous Perennial and Poisonous, its USDA zone range is 7a-10b, and all three dedicated-species sources otherwise describe an outdoor annual/perennial bedding, border or container plant.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note left null: no admissible source states a specific damage-onset temperature or describes a cool dormancy/rest period; NC State only gives a USDA hardiness zone range (7-10), which is a survival rating, not an onset temperature.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max left null: none of the admissible sources give numeric day/night temperature targets, humidity guidance, foot-candle light levels, or species-specific prose stating a maximum hours-of-direct-sun figure (NC State's Light field is a structured site-wide category legend, not species-specific hours prose, so it was used only for outdoor_sun_exposure, not direct_sun_hours_max).

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists only the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band with no closed ceiling, and RHS's dedicated Jacobaea maritima species page (as opposed to its 'Silver Dust' cultivar page, which was excluded as non-species-specific) carries no pH field at all to cross-check a ceiling against.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives an explicit watering statement or structured moisture field beyond MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' tag, which is mid-scale and per rule cannot support keep_moist; it is disclosed here only as a non-supporting counterpoint. NC State and MoBot's prose ('moist, well-drained soil' / 'average, evenly moist, well-drained soils') are soil-drainage descriptors, not watering-frequency statements.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis left null: this is an in-ground/container garden perennial and no admissible source frames watering as a dry-down or day-interval schedule.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength left null: none of the admissible sources discuss fertilizing this species.

The research record had parked this justification in unknowns with no citation naming the field.

RHS's Jacobaea maritima page carries a genus-level Botanical Details description of Jacobaea noting the genus is 'primarily known as being toxic to horses and cattle'. This batch's audit confirmed it is genus boilerplate by finding the identical paragraph on RHS's Senecio cineraria page, so it is not species-specific evidence and does not support toxic_to_pets; the species-level horse claim is separately carried by NC State's Problem for Horses tag, already cited.

RHS's Jacobaea maritima species page ('details' tab) does not carry a Position/Aspect/Soil/pH/Hardiness cultivation block; that data exists only on RHS's 'Silver Dust' cultivar page, which was excluded per the no-cultivar-page rule, so several cultivation-adjacent fields (soil pH ceiling, direct light needs beyond the NC State/MoBot sun fields) could not be cross-checked against RHS for the bare species.

Missouri Botanical Garden is internally split on the lead name: its structured Common Name field reads 'silver ragwort' (cited here) while its Noteworthy Characteristics prose opens by calling the plant dusty miller, per this batch's audit's live read. Plantfinder.mobot.org fails TLS certificate verification from the machine that landed this batch, and www.missouribotanicalgarden.org 301-redirects to it, so Missouri Botanical Garden could not be re-read here, so that prose sentence is disclosed here rather than quoted in name_note.

records.name_note: Admissible sources vary in the lead common name. NC State's dedicated Pelargonium peltatum page gives 'Ivy Geranium' as the first item of its Common Name(s) list, and RHS's dedicated species page likewise leads with 'ivy geranium' (listing 'hanging geranium, ivy-leaved geranium' under Other common names); this record leads with that name. Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated species page renders its Common Name field as 'Common Name: ivyleaf geranium'. Separately, Pelargonium peltatum is the trailing, ivy-leaved, hanging-basket type: Clemson HGIC's Annual Geranium factsheet gives it its own 'Ivy-Leaf Geraniums (Pelargonium peltatum)' section, kept distinct from the zonal Pelargonium x hortorum type covered elsewhere on that same factsheet.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Pelargonium peltatum page flags the record with 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' and carries a human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block: Poison Severity 'Low'; Poison Symptoms, reproduced in full, 'Vomiting, anorexia when consumed in quantity. Primarily GI upset, but also ataxia, muscle weakness, depression or hypothermia in larger exposures. Cats are most sensitive. Contact (allergic) dermatitis is mild.'; Poison Toxic Principle 'Geraniol, linalool'; Causes Contact Dermatitis 'Yes'; and Poison Part 'Leaves', which is the complete list — a single value. Separate from that human-scoped block, the Problems field carries exactly three tags — Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses — and it is the cats and dogs tags, not the human severity rating, that set toxic_to_pets true. NC State also carries this species under Whole Plant Traits > Plant Type as Poisonous, alongside Annual, Herbaceous Perennial and Houseplant. Neither Missouri Botanical Garden's nor Clemson HGIC's page for this species carries any toxicity or poison content, so there is no source disagreement on scope or edibility to disclose.
unknowns: No admissible source gave numeric day or night temperature ranges, or a stated chill-damage onset temperature, for this species; the closest statement found (Missouri Botanical Garden: best flowering occurs when nights are cool, in the 50s-60s F) is a bloom-quality note, not a damage-onset figure, so chill_damage_f, day_f_min/max, and night_f_min/max are left null.

No admissible source stated humidity needs or a percentage range, or light levels in foot-candles, for Pelargonium peltatum specifically, so humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, and light_fc_good are left null.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: the only numeric hour figure found (NC State's '2-6 hours' next to its Partial Shade Light tag) is that field's generic site-wide light-category legend text, not species-specific prose, and no admissible source gave a species-specific direct-sun-hours figure.

NC State's own page contains an internal conflict: its structured Light field is Partial Shade, but its cultivation prose says the plant 'requires full sun.' Both are used for outdoor_sun_exposure since each is independently sourced from that page, and Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Sun field ('Full sun to part shade') corroborates both ends.

soil_base is left null: NC State's Soil Texture/Soil Drainage tags (High Organic Matter, Sand; Good Drainage, Moist) describe an outdoor bed/container mix but do not map cleanly onto any single soil_base enum token, and no admissible source gave a specific potting-mix recommendation for this species.

soil_ph_min/max are left null: Missouri Botanical Garden's Culture section describes soil pH only qualitatively ('neutral to slightly alkaline pH') with no numeric bounds, and NC State's dedicated species page carries no Soil pH field at all.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est and water_estimate_basis are all left null because no admissible source states one of the four discrete regimes and the sources conflict. NC State: 'Once established, plants are drought-tolerant, but they grow better with moderate moisture. Plants in containers may be allowed to dry out between waterings.' — a drought-tolerance trait, which the rules bar from setting a regime. Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field is the mid-scale 'Water: Medium' with in-ground culture prose calling for regular watering during the growing season, and a mid-scale Water value never supports keep_moist. Clemson HGIC's Ivy-Leaf Geraniums bullet reads, with the page's own en dash, 'Moderate soil moisture – not too much and not too little'. RHS's species Cultivation adds a fourth, differently-shaped instruction: 'Irrigate moderately from spring to summer, and sparingly in winter allowing the compost to dry up between waterings.' Four sources, four shapes, no single enum token.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months and fertilize_strength are left null. Clemson HGIC's fertilizer text sits in its general 'Fertilizer Needs for Geraniums' section ('Geraniums usually require additional fertilizer during the growing season every four to six weeks.'), not inside the species-scoped Ivy-Leaf Geraniums section, so it is not used for this species and no day interval is computed from it. RHS's dedicated species page gives fertilizer type and season only — 'Apply a balanced liquid fertilizer during the growing season and switch to a high potassium fertilizer when flowering starts.' — with no interval, month list or strength, so the original entry's claim that no other admissible source gave fertilizer specifics is corrected here without changing the nulls.

RHS does carry a dedicated straight-species page for Pelargonium peltatum (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/76828/pelargonium-peltatum/details), whose H1 is the bare binomial and whose lead common name is 'ivy geranium'; the original entry's claim that RHS catalogs only trailing-type cultivars and groups is wrong. It is now cited here for scientific_name_accepted (Name Status 'Correct') and name_note. It changes no other value: its Hardiness 'H2' is a survival band ('tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5)', degrees C, per the page's own legend), not a damage-onset figure, so chill_damage_f stays null, and its pH field is the qualitative 'Neutral or Alkaline' with no numeric bounds, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max stay null.

NC State's Problems tags also include Problem for Horses, but per the rule that a citation naming only a different animal does not support toxic_to_pets, only the co-listed Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags were used to set toxic_to_pets=true.
